fields.description:
## Why this epic exists

On 2026-09-04 the Gerrit host went fully offline for 41 minutes. Detection worked: ten alarms
fired within seven minutes. **Explanation did not.** The cause had to be reconstructed afterwards
from EBS I/O counters, and the direct evidence — kernel logs — was never captured and is now
permanently gone.

That gap is not incidental. It follows from a single structural property:

> **Every signal we have about the host is produced BY the host.**
> When the host degrades, the observation degrades with it — and the failure that most needs
> explaining is precisely the one that destroys its own evidence.

This epic makes observability survive the thing it observes.

## What tonight established, concretely

- **No off-box log destination exists.** 15 CloudWatch log groups in the account, ALL belonging to
  unrelated projects. The Gerrit host's logs live only in on-box journald and die with it. The
  2026-09-02 five-hour outage had the identical gap; nothing changed between incidents.
- **EC2 console output is not a substitute.** During the incident it returned bytes timestamped
  two days stale; after the recovery stop/start it returns EMPTY. (Correction 2026-11-03: the
  `--latest` form returns a current snapshot on this Nitro instance; the stale bytes came from the
  cached form. It is a pre-restart capture, not a log.)
- **Three metrics have been silently dead for 7+ days** — `disk_used_percent{mount=/var/gerrit}`,
  `gerrit_healthy`, `reviewbot_healthy` — making their alarms unfalsifiable. And `list-metrics`
  still shows the NAMES, so every superficial check reports the telemetry as present.
- **The primary data volume could not be confirmed mounted** during recovery. The best available
  answer was inference from EBS read counts (49,834 vs 49 on a known-raw volume). Correct, almost
  certainly — but an inference, not a measurement.
- **The cause was IOPS saturation, on a dimension nothing alarms on.** Root reads pinned flat at
  ~2,500 IOPS for 30 minutes at only 47% disk FULL. Neither disk-space alarms nor the (absent)
  memory alarm would have caught it.

## The distinction this epic turns on

**Detection and diagnosis are different capabilities, and we only built the first.**

`herbal-garish-monkey` did real work: it converted dead-man silence into a page across 15 alarms,
and that is what caught tonight's outage in seven minutes. Nothing here supersedes it. But "the
host is gone" is where the information ends. There is no path from an alarm to a cause, and with
no off-box evidence, restoring service DESTROYS the only record — forcing every incident into
"restore quickly or diagnose, never both". That tradeoff is an artefact of missing telemetry, not
a law of nature.

## Success for this epic

A future unexplained outage can be explained afterwards, without the host being alive, and without
choosing between recovery speed and root cause.

Explicit non-goal: a general observability platform. The bar is "an incident can be explained",
not "we have dashboards". Retention costs money — note the account already carries 15 log groups
with `retentionInDays: None`, a pattern not to inherit.

## Children

- `fab-dismal-haddock` — no off-box logs; an outage produced no diagnosable evidence. Owns every
  criterion below.
- `enviable-beloved-buffalo` — closed `not_a_bug`: the three metrics were measured publishing on
  2026-09-20 and 2026-10-24. Its detector capability moved to `bold-causative-nandoo`, which is
  outside this epic.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Host logs survive the host: journald (kernel, the rebar containers, nginx, systemd unit
      failures) and nginx `error.log` reach a CloudWatch log group with an explicit, finite
      retention, verified by reading the last lines from off-box after a source stops
      (`fab-dismal-haddock`).
- [ ] At least one host-health observation originates off the host, so a dead host cannot
      silence its own observer, verified by its alarm state while host publishing is absent
      (`fab-dismal-haddock`).
- [ ] A silently stopped log pipeline pages rather than looking configured: an alarm on the log
      group's incoming events treats missing data as breaching (`fab-dismal-haddock`).
- [ ] A documented runbook path leads from "an alarm fired" to "what the box was doing" without
      the box alive, and captures `get-console-output --latest` before any restart with its added
      downtime stated (`fab-dismal-haddock`).

## Related, tracked elsewhere — do NOT duplicate

- `witted-invisible-roan` owns the missing MEMORY alarm (`mem_available_percent` is
  measurement-only). Memory exhaustion is the leading hypothesis for tonight's cascade.
- `smudgeless-friendless-longspur` owns IOPS saturation detection and the finding that epic 6202
  bounds disk SPACE, not IOPS.
- `unamused-cloudy-junebug` owns the missing `/var/gerrit` mount assertion — which
  `enviable-beloved-buffalo` explains cannot currently be implemented as intended, because the
  metric it would read is dead.
- `herbal-garish-monkey` owns `treat_missing_data` correctness, including the unenumerated
  `missing` value on the two EC2 status-check alarms that stayed silent through tonight's outage.

The boundary is deliberate: those four are about ALARMING on conditions. This epic is about being
able to EXPLAIN what happened, which is a different capability and fails in a different way.
